title: The King of Good Times
hook: Vijay Mallya's airline was India's most glamorous. It never made a profit. Can you make it fly?

profit.label: Cash
profit.hint: Money in the bank to keep the planes flying

future.label: Strength
future.hint: How likely your airline is to last

intro.text: Bengaluru, 2004. You run a big Indian drinks group, and you have a new dream: an airline with your brand's name on every plane. New Airbus jets are already on order, and the first arrive next year.

s_goal.text: But flying in India has just changed. A new low-fare airline has made tickets much cheaper: Delhi to Mumbai cost over ₹6,500 last year and can now cost under ₹2,000. Your goal is to build an airline India loves and make it pay before the money runs out.

d1.title: What kind of airline?
d1.setup: Your first planes arrive in May 2005. Before then, you must decide what flyers will get for their money. That choice will shape almost every cost you have.
d1.question: What kind of airline will you launch?
d1.advisor: Our brand stands for the good life, but flyers now know how cheap a ticket can be. We need to decide what they will pay extra for.

options.label: Go premium: new jets, seat screens, good food and top service for everyone, with higher fares.
options.outcome: On 9 May 2005 your first flights take off. Flyers love the new jets, the seat screens and the service, and people praise its service. But every seat costs a lot to fly, and in the first 15 months you lose ₹337 crore.
options.why: The service won hearts, but in a fare war few flyers pay top prices. Your costs were high, and your fares could not cover them.
options.better: Keep costs as low as the cheapest airline, grow only on routes that pay, and give flyers a simple reason to choose you, like leaving on time.
options.takeaway: In 2004 you built a costly airline just as fares were crashing.

options.label: Go cheapest: offer India's lowest fares, even below cost for a while, and win flyers on price.
options.outcome: Your planes fill up and the papers love your fares. But you lose money on every seat, and the low-fare airline cuts its prices too. Soon you are both burning cash to win the same flyers.
options.why: Selling below cost only works if you can outlast your rival. Here you both bled money, and nobody won.
options.better: Keep costs as low as the cheapest airline, grow only on routes that pay, and give flyers a simple reason to choose you, like leaving on time.
options.takeaway: In 2004 you started a price war you could not win.

options.label: Go lean: one type of plane, simple service and fair fares, and grow only on routes that pay.
options.outcome: Your airline launches with less glamour but lower costs. Each route has to earn its place, and in the first year you lose far less than your rivals. Flyers start to trust you for cheap fares and on-time flights.
options.why: Low costs let you survive a fare war that sinks others. Glamour is nice, but cash keeps planes flying.
options.takeaway: In 2004 you kept costs low, so a fare war couldn't sink you.

d2.title: Buy the rival?

setup.text: It is 2007. Your airline is loved but losing money: ₹337 crore in its first 15 months and ₹420 crore in the year after. Now Air Deccan, India's first low-fare airline, is looking for an investor.
It is 2007. Fares are still falling and money is tight for every airline. Air Deccan, India's first low-fare airline, is losing money and looking for an investor.

d2.question: What do you do about Air Deccan?
d2.advisor: Deccan brings flyers and routes, but it is losing money too. Buying it could make us bigger, or make our problems bigger.

options.label: Leave Deccan alone and fix your own airline first, even if another rival buys it.
options.outcome: You let Deccan go and keep your money for your own airline. You close routes that lose money and keep a tight hold on costs. It isn't exciting, but your losses shrink year by year.
options.why: When you're losing money, buying another airline that loses money only doubles the problem. Fixing your own costs came first.
options.takeaway: In 2007 you fixed your own airline before buying someone else's.

options.label: Buy a quarter of Air Deccan for ₹550 crore, then work towards joining the two airlines.
options.outcome: In May 2007 you buy 26% of Air Deccan for ₹550 crore. The next year the two airlines become one company, and Deccan is renamed Kingfisher Red. Now you run a costly airline and a cheap one, and both lose money.
options.why: You spent money you didn't have on an airline that also lost money. Two loss-makers together don't make a profit.
options.better: Fix your own costs first, and buy a rival only once your own airline makes money.
options.takeaway: In 2007 you bought a second loss-making airline while your own was losing money.

options.label: Build your own low-fare airline under a new name, using some of your new planes.
options.outcome: Your new low-fare brand takes a year to get going and fights Deccan for the same flyers. It loses money too, but at least you control its costs, and you didn't pay ₹550 crore to start it.
options.why: A second brand split your money and your focus at a time when your main airline still needed fixing.
options.better: Fix the airline you have first. Growth can wait until it pays its way.
options.takeaway: In 2007 you started a second airline before the first one made money.

d3.title: Fly abroad now?

setup.text: It is early 2008. India lets an airline fly abroad only after five years of flying at home, and your airline has three. But Air Deccan, which is now joining your company, started flying in 2003 and passes five years this summer.
It is early 2008. India lets an airline fly abroad only after five years of flying at home, and your airline has three. Long routes can earn more than short ones, but the big planes cost a fortune.

d3.question: How do you go after flights abroad?
d3.advisor: Flying to London would lift our image, but big planes need a lot of money. We could also wait, or reach foreign flyers another way.

options.label: Merge into an older airline that will soon pass five years of flying, then start London flights this year.

outcome.text: Your airline merges into Deccan's older company, and on 3 September 2008 your first flight leaves Bangalore for London. It's a proud day. But the big long-route planes cost a fortune, and fuel prices have already doubled.

You merge into an older airline to borrow its years, and your first London flight leaves in late 2008. It's a proud day. But the big long-route planes cost a fortune, and fuel prices have already doubled.

options.why: Flying abroad won you pride, but it tied up cash in costly planes just as fuel prices soared.
options.better: Wait until your flights at home make money, then go abroad.
options.takeaway: In 2008 you went abroad before your home routes made money.

options.label: Wait until your own five years are up, and keep spending the cash on your routes at home.
options.outcome: You stay at home and spend the money on your short routes. It feels small next to a rival's London flights, but it leaves you cash in the bank when fuel prices jump later that year.
options.why: Waiting looked timid, but it kept your cash safe for the storm that was coming.
options.takeaway: In 2008 you waited, and kept the cash you'd soon need.

options.label: Skip your own long routes, and sell foreign trips through partner airlines for a small fee each.
options.outcome: Partner airlines fly your flyers abroad and pay you a small fee. It earns a little and costs almost nothing, but rivals grow abroad while you stay at home.
options.why: It was safe, but it also kept you small while your home routes still lost money.
options.better: Use the quiet time to fix the losses at home, so you're ready to fly abroad on your own later.
options.takeaway: In 2008 you played it safe abroad but left the losses at home alone.

d4.title: The fuel shock
d4.setup: Late 2008. Jet fuel now costs more than twice what it did in 2003, and fewer people are flying as the world slides into a slump. Almost every airline in India is losing money, and the oil companies want to be paid.
d4.question: How do you get through the slump?
d4.advisor: Cutting flights could save cash, but it also makes the airline look weaker. Keeping them flying protects our size, but empty seats cost money.

options.label: Keep every plane flying and cut fares to fill more seats, hoping fuel gets cheaper again.
options.outcome: Your seats fill up, but each one now loses more money than before. Fuel stays expensive, and the losses grow into a hole too deep to climb out of.
options.why: Cheap fares filled seats but deepened the losses. In a slump, flying more just means losing more.
options.better: Shrink fast: park planes, close losing routes and raise new cash while you still can.
options.takeaway: In 2008 you kept flying full and losing money, hoping fuel would get cheaper.

options.label: Team up with Jet Airways, your biggest rival, to share costs, and send back your biggest planes.
options.outcome: In October 2008 you and Jet Airways agree to share flight codes, crews and ground work. You send back five big long-route planes and put off 32 new ones. It saves money, but the losses keep coming: about ₹1,600 crore that year and the same again the next.
options.why: Sharing costs helped, but it was small next to your losses, and you kept almost every route flying.
options.better: Cut much deeper and faster, and raise new cash from owners while you still can.
options.takeaway: In 2008 you cut costs, but not nearly enough for the size of the losses.

options.label: Shrink hard: park planes, close weak routes, cut jobs and raise new cash from owners.
options.outcome: It's a painful year. Planes sit parked, routes close and many staff leave. But your losses shrink, and the new cash from owners keeps you safe through the slump.
options.why: Shrinking hurt, but it matched your airline to the market and kept you alive until flyers came back.
options.takeaway: In 2008 you shrank fast and raised cash, so the slump didn't sink you.

text.text: By 2010 the slump is easing. You cut hard and your airline is smaller, but you still owe the banks a lot, and you'll need fresh money to grow again.
By 2010 your airline has lost money every year since it began. You now owe about ₹8,000 crore to 18 lenders, most of them government banks, and the interest alone eats your cash.

d5.title: The banks
d5.setup: Your lenders are worried, and so are your staff. You need fresh money or more time to pay what you owe, and there are only a few ways to get it.
d5.question: Where does the money come from?
d5.advisor: Every choice costs us something: control, size or more of the airline. We need the one that gives us the best chance to keep flying.

options.label: Sell a big share to a new investor for fresh cash, even if you give up control.
options.outcome: A new investor brings fresh cash and new bosses to answer to. You no longer call every shot, but the airline can pay its bills and fly through the next crisis.
options.why: Giving up control hurt your pride, but it brought real money in instead of just more time.
options.takeaway: In 2010 you gave up control to bring in fresh cash.

options.label: Shrink into a smaller airline by selling planes and keeping only routes that make money.
options.outcome: Your airline gets smaller but steadier: fewer planes, fewer routes, smaller losses. The glamour is gone, but you can pay your people.
options.why: Shrinking stopped the bleeding, but without new money you had little room to grow or to survive another shock.
options.better: Shrink and bring in a new investor, so you have both lower costs and fresh cash.
options.takeaway: In 2010 you shrank to survive, but brought in no new money.

options.label: Ask the banks to turn part of your loans into shares and cut your interest, while you keep control.
options.outcome: The banks agree. In 2011 they take 23.4% of your airline in exchange for ₹750 crore of loans, paying about 60% more per share than the market price. Your interest is cut and you get nine years to pay. But the losses grow, and in 2011-12 you lose ₹2,328 crore.
options.why: The deal bought time but fixed nothing. You kept control and kept losing money, and now the banks were tied to your airline.
options.better: Bring in fresh money from an investor and cut costs, even if it costs you control.
options.takeaway: In 2010 you bought time from the banks instead of fixing the airline.

s2012.text: 2012. The money has run out. Most of your planes are parked, your staff have gone months without pay, and the banks have stopped lending. Then your staff stop work.

d6.title: Staff unpaid, planes on the ground
d6.setup: October 2012. About 4,000 staff haven't been paid for months, and your flights have stopped. The regulator gives you until 20 October to show a plan, backed by money, to fly safely again.
d6.question: What do you do now?
d6.advisor: We need money and people back at work before we can fly again. Each path could save something, but none comes without a heavy cost.

options.label: Lock out the striking staff, keep the airline shut, and search for an investor to fund a restart.
options.outcome: No investor comes in time. On 20 October 2012 the regulator suspends your licence. At the end of the year your flying permit lapses, and in 2013 your flying rights are taken away. Your planes never fly again.
options.why: Waiting for a rescue while staff went unpaid used up the last trust your staff and the regulator had in you.
options.better: Pay staff first, even by selling things you love, and restart small with a plan the regulator can trust.
options.takeaway: In 2012 you waited for a rescue while staff went unpaid.

options.label: Sell other businesses you own to pay staff first, then restart with only a few planes.
options.outcome: Selling your other businesses hurts, but staff are paid and come back to work. You restart with a handful of planes. It's a small airline now, but it's flying.
options.why: Paying people first won back trust, and a small airline that flies beats a big one that doesn't.
options.takeaway: In 2012 you paid your staff first and restarted small.

options.label: Hand the airline to the banks and close it in an orderly way, sharing what's left with staff and lenders.
options.outcome: The banks take over and wind the airline down slowly. Staff and lenders get part of what they're owed. It's an ending, but a calm one.
options.why: Closing calmly was honest, but it gave up on any chance to keep flying.
options.better: Pay staff first and restart small, if you can find the money by selling other things.
options.takeaway: In 2012 you closed the airline calmly instead of fighting for it.

legend.title: Still flying high
legend.text: Years later your airline is still in the sky. It isn't the flashiest one, but it pays its bills, its staff are paid on time, and flyers trust it. You built an airline that lasted.

text.text: Your airline is gone, but it ended calmly. Staff and banks got part of what they were owed, and nobody was left waiting for years.
Your airline is smaller than your dream, but it's still flying. Staff are paid and the banks are calm. Not every dream fits the market, and you changed yours in time.
Your airline is grounded for good. It never made a profit in a single year. The staff wait years for their pay, and the banks go to court to get their money back.
Your airline runs out of money and stops flying. Staff go unpaid, and the banks go to court for what they're owed.

fired.title: The board lets you go
fired.text: One costly call too many. The board and the banks lose faith in you, and they hand the airline to someone else to save.

realHistory: Kingfisher Airlines launched in May 2005 as a premium airline and never made a profit in a single year. In 2007 it paid ₹550 crore for 26% of Air Deccan, merged with it, and used Deccan's longer history to start flying to London in 2008. Fuel prices doubled, losses grew, and in 2011 banks swapped ₹750 crore of loans for 23.4% of the airline. About 4,000 staff went unpaid for months in 2012. The regulator suspended Kingfisher's licence on 20 October 2012, and it never flew again. Banks said they were owed more than ₹9,000 crore; in 2017 a debt tribunal ordered ₹6,203 crore plus interest to be repaid. The chairman, Vijay Mallya, left India on 2 March 2016. In January 2019 a Mumbai court declared him a fugitive economic offender, which he challenged in the Bombay High Court. UK courts approved his extradition, but he has not been sent back. The government says ₹14,131 crore has been recovered from his assets; he says that is double what he owed, and that he did nothing wrong.
